questions.prompt: A conveyor-speed loop uses only a proportional gain. A constant extra load is added and the speed settles slightly below the setpoint. Which statement is correct?
options: P control needs nonzero error to supply the holding effort, so an offset remains; integral action removes it.
The gain is too high, so the loop overshoots and settles low; reducing the gain removes the offset.
The derivative term is missing; adding derivative action supplies the holding effort and removes the offset.
The offset is just measurement noise on the speed sensor and averages out over a long enough run.
questions.explanation: With u = Kp e and a constant load, equilibrium needs u > 0 so e cannot be zero. Only an integrator (or a load feedforward) supplies the effort at zero error.

questions.prompt: An arm joint is commanded to a target that needs more torque than the motor can give. The integrator keeps accumulating. When the joint finally arrives, what happens with a plain integrator?
options: It overshoots, because the stored integral keeps the command at the limit until negative error unwinds it.
It oscillates only if Kd is nonzero, since the derivative term is what reacts to the saturated output.
It never leaves the limit, because the integral is reset to zero as soon as the output y reaches r.
It stops exactly on target, because clipping the output also clips the integral state so nothing is stored.
questions.explanation: Clipping the output does not clip the integral state. The excess integral must be unwound by an error of the opposite sign: windup overshoot.

questions.prompt: Position noise has sigma = 0.02 rad per sample (independent), Delta t = 0.01 s, Kd = 0.25. A raw finite difference feeds the D term. Standard deviation of the D contribution to u (2 decimals)?

rubric: Chooses PI (or PI + feedforward) and explains why the offset needs an integrator.
Includes anti-windup (clamp or back-calculation) and a limit on D or none.
Names logged signals (u_raw, u, integral, error) and a rejection criterion.
